questions.stem: Which feature is found in RNA nucleotides but not in DNA nucleotides?
options: A deoxyribose sugar and the base thymine
A phosphate group and the base adenine
A ribose sugar and the base thymine
A ribose sugar and the base uracil
questions.explanation: RNA nucleotides contain ribose and can carry uracil, which replaces the thymine found in DNA. Pairing ribose with thymine is the tempting mix-up: thymine belongs to DNA, so it does not appear in mRNA, tRNA or rRNA. Phosphate and adenine are common to both nucleic acids.

questions.stem: Which form of RNA carries a specific amino acid to the ribosome and has an anticodon?
options: Messenger RNA (mRNA)
Ribosomal RNA (rRNA)
Pre-mRNA
Transfer RNA (tRNA)
questions.explanation: Each tRNA molecule binds one particular amino acid and has an anticodon that pairs with a complementary mRNA codon. mRNA carries the codons themselves, not anticodons, and rRNA combines with proteins to form the ribosome.

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 22% guanine. What percentage of its bases are thymine?
questions.explanation: Guanine pairs with cytosine, so cytosine is also 22% and G + C is 44%. The remaining 56% is shared equally by adenine and thymine, giving 28% thymine. Answering 56% stops one step short, because that figure is A and T together.

questions.stem: Why are the two strands of a DNA molecule described as antiparallel?
options: They twist in opposite directions, forming two separate helices
They run in opposite directions, one 5′ to 3′ and the other 3′ to 5′
They are held apart by covalent bonds between the bases on each strand
They carry different sugars, deoxyribose on one strand and ribose on the other
questions.explanation: Antiparallel means the sugar-phosphate backbones point in opposite directions, so one strand runs 5′ to 3′ while its partner runs 3′ to 5′. The bases on opposite strands are joined by hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds, and both strands contain deoxyribose.

questions.stem: The genetic code is described as degenerate. What does this mean?
options: Each codon is made up of three nucleotides in a row
Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon
Each codon can code for more than one amino acid
The same codons code for the same amino acids in almost all organisms
questions.explanation: Degenerate (or redundant) means several codons can specify the same amino acid: there are 61 codons for 20 amino acids. Using the same code across organisms describes universality, and three nucleotides per codon describes a triplet code. No codon codes for more than one amino acid, which is what keeps translation unambiguous.

questions.stem: During transcription, which enzyme binds to the promoter and synthesises a complementary RNA strand?
options: DNA polymerase
DNA ligase
Reverse transcriptase
RNA polymerase
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase binds at the promoter, unwinds the DNA and builds pre-mRNA using the template strand. DNA polymerase builds DNA, not RNA, and is the enzyme of replication and PCR.

questions.stem: The template strand of a section of DNA reads 3′ TAC GGA TTC 5′. What is the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from it?
options: 5′ AUG CCU AAG 3′
5′ ATG CCT AAG 3′
5′ UAC GGA UUC 3′
3′ AUG CCU AAG 5′
questions.explanation: mRNA is complementary to the template strand, with uracil pairing with adenine, so TAC GGA TTC gives AUG CCU AAG. It is built 5′ to 3′, antiparallel to the template. The sequence with T instead of U is the coding strand of DNA, not mRNA.

questions.stem: In a eukaryotic cell, which change happens to pre-mRNA during RNA processing?
options: Thymine bases are replaced with uracil so it can leave the nucleus
The codons are translated into amino acids before it leaves the nucleus
Introns are removed and a methyl-G cap and poly-A tail are added
Exons are removed and the introns are joined to form mature mRNA
questions.explanation: RNA processing splices out introns, joins the exons, and adds a methyl-G cap at the 5′ end and a poly-A tail at the 3′ end. Removing the exons reverses the roles: exons are the expressed sequences that stay. Pre-mRNA never contained thymine, because it is made with uracil from the start.

questions.stem: An mRNA codon reads 5′ GCU 3′. What is the anticodon on the tRNA that pairs with it?
options: 3′ CGA 5′
3′ GCU 5′
3′ CGT 5′
3′ UCG 5′
questions.explanation: The anticodon is complementary and antiparallel to the codon, so 5′ GCU 3′ pairs with 3′ CGA 5′. An anticodon cannot contain thymine because tRNA is RNA. Reversing the codon is not the same as finding its complement.

questions.stem: A point mutation changes a DNA triplet so that the mRNA codon CUU becomes CUC. Both codons code for leucine. Which property of the genetic code explains why the protein is unchanged?
options: The code is universal
The code is a triplet code
The code is non-overlapping
The code is degenerate
questions.explanation: Because the code is degenerate, CUU and CUC both specify leucine, so this silent mutation does not change the amino acid sequence. Universality is about the same code working across species, which is why human genes can be expressed in bacteria, and says nothing about this substitution.

questions.stem: A pre-mRNA molecule contains four exons and three introns. Different cell types join different combinations of its exons. What is the main consequence for the organism?
options: Introns are translated in some cell types but not in others
The gene is replicated differently in each type of cell
One gene can code for several different polypeptides
Each cell type expresses a different version of the gene's DNA
questions.explanation: Alternative splicing joins different sets of exons from the same pre-mRNA, so one gene gives rise to several polypeptides. This is one reason the proteome is larger than the number of genes. The DNA itself is identical in each cell type; the difference arises after transcription.

questions.stem: During translation, what bond forms between adjacent amino acids, and where does this happen?
options: A peptide bond, in the nucleus
A phosphodiester bond, at the Golgi apparatus
A peptide bond, at the ribosome
A hydrogen bond, at the ribosome
questions.explanation: The ribosome joins amino acids with peptide bonds in condensation reactions as each tRNA delivers its amino acid. Hydrogen bonds hold codon and anticodon together briefly but do not link amino acids. Translation takes place in the cytosol or on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, not in the nucleus.

questions.stem: In a eukaryotic gene, what is the role of the promoter region?
options: It is the coding section that is translated into amino acids
It is where RNA polymerase binds to begin transcription
It is where a repressor protein binds to block transcription
It is a non-coding section removed from pre-mRNA by splicing
questions.explanation: The promoter lies upstream of the coding region and is the binding site for RNA polymerase. A repressor binding to block transcription describes an operator, which is found in prokaryotic operons. A non-coding section removed by splicing is an intron.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares exons and introns?
options: Exons are kept in mature mRNA; introns are removed from pre-mRNA
Introns are kept in mature mRNA; exons are removed from pre-mRNA
Exons are found only in prokaryotes; introns are found only in eukaryotes
Exons are transcribed into mRNA; introns are never transcribed at all
questions.explanation: Both exons and introns are transcribed into pre-mRNA, then the introns are spliced out and the exons are joined. The claim that introns are never transcribed is the common error: they are copied first and removed during RNA processing. Exons occur in all genes, while introns are typical of eukaryotic genes.

questions.stem: In the trp operon of Escherichia coli, what do the structural genes trpE, trpD, trpC, trpB and trpA code for?
options: The repressor protein that binds to the operator
Enzymes that break down tryptophan for energy
Proteins that transport tryptophan into the cell
Enzymes that synthesise the amino acid tryptophan
questions.explanation: The five structural genes code for the enzymes of the pathway that makes tryptophan. The repressor protein is coded by a separate regulatory gene, trpR, located away from the operon.

questions.stem: An E. coli cell is growing in a medium rich in tryptophan. What happens at the trp operon?
options: Tryptophan binds the repressor, which then binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase
Tryptophan binds the operator directly, which stops the repressor from being made
The repressor binds tryptophan and leaves the operator, so transcription speeds up
Tryptophan binds RNA polymerase, which then cuts the operon's structural genes
questions.explanation: Tryptophan acts as a corepressor: binding changes the repressor's shape so it can attach to the operator, which stops RNA polymerase transcribing the structural genes. The cell saves energy by not making enzymes for something it already has. Tryptophan does not bind the operator itself.

questions.stem: A mutant E. coli strain makes a repressor that cannot bind tryptophan. How will transcription of the trp structural genes respond when tryptophan is plentiful?
options: It continues only at low levels, because RNA polymerase cannot bind the promoter
It continues, because the repressor cannot become active and bind the operator
It stops, because tryptophan binds the operator in place of the repressor
It stops, because the inactive repressor permanently blocks the promoter
questions.explanation: The repressor needs tryptophan bound to it before it can attach to the operator. A repressor that cannot bind tryptophan stays inactive, so RNA polymerase keeps transcribing the genes even though the product is not needed. The repressor never blocks the promoter in its inactive form.

questions.stem: In the trp operon, attenuation can stop transcription early when tryptophan levels are high. What causes this?
options: The repressor binds the leader sequence, so the ribosome cannot attach to the mRNA
The ribosome moves quickly through the leader, so a terminator loop forms in the mRNA
The ribosome stalls at tryptophan codons in the leader, so a terminator loop forms
Tryptophan binds the leader mRNA, so RNA polymerase cannot leave the promoter
questions.explanation: When tryptophan is plentiful, charged tryptophan tRNAs let the ribosome move through the leader sequence quickly, and the mRNA folds into a terminator hairpin that ends transcription. A stalled ribosome is what happens when tryptophan is scarce, and that allows the anti-terminator loop to form so transcription continues.

questions.stem: Which level of protein structure is the sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds?
options: Primary structure
Secondary structure
Tertiary structure
Quaternary structure
questions.explanation: Primary structure is the order of amino acids in the polypeptide chain. Secondary structure is the local folding into alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds, which depends on that sequence.

questions.stem: Which part of an amino acid varies between the 20 amino acids and determines its chemical properties?
options: The amine group
The carboxyl group
The central carbon atom
The R group
questions.explanation: Every amino acid has the same central carbon, amine group and carboxyl group; only the R group differs. The R groups decide how a polypeptide folds, because they form the hydrophobic interactions, ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds and disulfide bridges of tertiary structure.

questions.stem: An enzyme loses its function when a single amino acid in its primary structure is replaced by one with a very different R group. What is the best explanation?
options: The new amino acid stops the gene from being transcribed
The new amino acid makes the enzyme bind more than one substrate
The changed R group alters folding, so the active site changes shape
The changed R group breaks every peptide bond in the polypeptide
questions.explanation: R groups interact to give the tertiary structure, so a very different R group can change how the chain folds and alter the shape of the active site. The substrate then no longer fits. Peptide bonds in the backbone are unaffected; the change is in folding, not in how the chain is linked.

questions.stem: What is the proteome of an organism?
options: The set of enzymes in one biochemical pathway
The sequence of amino acids in one protein
All the proteins expressed by the organism
The complete set of genes carried by the organism
questions.explanation: The proteome is all the proteins expressed by a cell, tissue or organism. The complete set of genes is the genome. The proteome changes over time and between cell types, while the genome is the same in nearly every cell.

questions.stem: Human liver cells and skin cells have the same genome but different proteomes. What best explains this?
options: Different genes are expressed in each cell type
Each cell type has lost the genes it does not use
Each cell type translates its introns in different ways
Skin cells copy their DNA less accurately than liver cells
questions.explanation: Specialised cells keep the whole genome but switch on different genes, so they make different sets of proteins. Cells do not lose unused genes, and introns are removed rather than translated.

questions.stem: A protein to be exported from a cell is made by ribosomes attached to which organelle?
options: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Mitochondrion
Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Golgi apparatus
questions.explanation: Ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum feed the growing polypeptide into its lumen, where folding begins. The Golgi apparatus is the next stop, where the protein is modified and packaged, but it has no ribosomes.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the protein secretory pathway?
options: Golgi apparatus → transport vesicle → rough ER → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane
Rough ER → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane → transport vesicle → Golgi apparatus
Nucleus → Golgi apparatus → rough ER → transport vesicle → plasma membrane
Rough ER → transport vesicle → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane
questions.explanation: The protein is made at the rough ER, carried in a transport vesicle to the Golgi apparatus for modification and packaging, then carried in a secretory vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane by exocytosis. Putting the Golgi before the rough ER reverses the first two steps.

questions.stem: Cells are given a drug that stops vesicles budding from the Golgi apparatus. A hormone normally secreted by the cells is tracked. Where would it most likely accumulate?
options: In the nucleus
In the cytosol, free of any organelle
On free ribosomes in the cytosol
In the Golgi apparatus
questions.explanation: The hormone still passes from the rough ER to the Golgi, but with no secretory vesicles budding off it cannot leave, so it builds up there. Proteins for export are inside the endomembrane system, not loose in the cytosol, and they never enter the nucleus.

questions.stem: Which enzyme joins two DNA fragments by forming bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone?
options: DNA polymerase
RNA polymerase
DNA ligase
Restriction endonuclease
questions.explanation: DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides, sealing fragments together, for example a gene into a plasmid. A restriction endonuclease does the opposite: it cuts the backbone at a recognition site.

questions.stem: The restriction enzyme EcoRI cuts the sequence 5′ GAATTC 3′ between G and A on each strand. What kind of ends does it produce?
options: Blunt ends with no single-stranded overhangs
Sticky ends with long double-stranded overhangs
Blunt ends with a single overhanging base
Sticky ends with short single-stranded overhangs
questions.explanation: Cutting between G and A on both antiparallel strands leaves staggered cuts, so each end has a four-base single-stranded overhang (AATT). These sticky ends can base-pair with any fragment cut by the same enzyme. Blunt ends come from enzymes that cut both strands at the same point.

questions.stem: A scientist cuts a plasmid with EcoRI and a gene with SmaI, which produces blunt ends. Ligase is added but very few recombinant plasmids form. What is the most likely reason?
options: SmaI cuts the plasmid's antibiotic resistance gene
EcoRI cuts only RNA, not double-stranded DNA
The ends produced by the two enzymes are not complementary
Ligase can only join fragments cut by SmaI
questions.explanation: Sticky ends from EcoRI cannot base-pair with blunt ends from SmaI, so the gene and the plasmid do not line up for ligase to seal. That is why the same restriction enzyme is normally used on both, giving complementary sticky ends. Ligase can join blunt ends too, just less efficiently.

questions.stem: What does DNA polymerase need before it can begin adding nucleotides to a single strand of DNA?
options: A primer with a free 3′ end bound to the strand
A promoter region that RNA polymerase has bound
A sticky end produced by a restriction enzyme
A ribosome attached at the start codon
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase can only extend an existing strand, adding nucleotides to a free 3′ end, so a short primer must first bind to the template. In PCR, two primers flank the region to be copied. A promoter is needed by RNA polymerase in transcription, not by DNA polymerase.

questions.stem: In bacteria, what is the natural function of the CRISPR-Cas9 system?
options: Regulation of the trp operon when nutrients run low
Defence against bacteriophages by cutting their DNA
Repair of the bacterium's own DNA after mutation
Transfer of plasmids between neighbouring bacteria
questions.explanation: CRISPR-Cas9 is an adaptive defence: the bacterium stores spacers copied from earlier phage infections and uses them to guide Cas9 to cut matching phage DNA if the phage returns. It is not a repair system for the bacterium's own DNA.

questions.stem: In CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, what determines where in the genome Cas9 cuts?
options: The guide RNA, which is complementary to the target sequence
The Cas9 protein, which recognises one fixed sequence only
The restriction site, which is palindromic and four bases long
The primer, which binds next to the start codon of the gene
questions.explanation: Scientists design a guide RNA whose sequence matches the target, and it leads Cas9 to that site, next to a PAM sequence, where Cas9 cuts both strands. Changing the guide RNA retargets the same Cas9, which is what makes the tool so flexible. A fixed palindromic recognition site describes restriction enzymes.

questions.stem: Bacteria store spacers copied from phage DNA in their own CRISPR array, yet Cas9 does not cut the array. Which feature prevents this?
options: The array is protected inside the nucleus of the bacterium
Cas9 is made only after all of the phage DNA has been cut
Cas9 cuts only next to a PAM sequence, which the array lacks
The spacers are stored as RNA, which Cas9 cannot recognise
questions.explanation: Cas9 needs a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) beside the target before it will cut. The phage DNA has a PAM next to the matching sequence, but the copy stored in the bacterium's CRISPR array does not, so the bacterium's own DNA is spared. Bacteria have no nucleus, and spacers are stored as DNA.

questions.stem: After Cas9 cuts both strands of a target gene, the cell repairs the break and small insertions or deletions often result. How is this used in genome editing?
options: To add a poly-A tail to the gene's mature mRNA
To knock out the gene by disrupting its reading frame
To copy the gene many times for gel electrophoresis
To join the gene into a plasmid with sticky ends
questions.explanation: Error-prone repair of the cut often adds or removes a few nucleotides, which can shift the reading frame and silence the gene. Supplying a template DNA as well lets a new sequence be inserted instead. Copying a gene many times is the job of PCR.

questions.stem: In PCR, what happens at about 95°C?
options: Taq polymerase extends the new strands from the primers
The DNA fragments are sorted by size in a gel
The double-stranded DNA separates into single strands
The primers anneal to the single strands of DNA
questions.explanation: Heating to about 95°C breaks the hydrogen bonds between bases, denaturing the DNA. Cooling to about 50–60°C lets the primers anneal, and about 72°C is the working temperature for Taq polymerase to extend the strands.

questions.stem: Why is Taq polymerase used in PCR instead of human DNA polymerase?
options: It is heat-stable and is not denatured at 95°C
It can copy RNA as well as DNA in each cycle
It does not need primers to begin synthesis
It cuts DNA at sites next to the primers
questions.explanation: Taq polymerase comes from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium of hot springs, so it survives the repeated 95°C denaturing step. A human enzyme would be denatured in the first cycle. Taq still needs primers, like every DNA polymerase.

questions.stem: A PCR starts with one double-stranded copy of a target sequence. Assuming every cycle doubles the DNA, how many copies are present after 10 cycles?
questions.explanation: Each cycle doubles the number of copies, so 10 cycles give 2¹⁰ = 1024 copies. The answer 512 is 2⁹, one doubling short, and 2048 is one doubling too many; 20 comes from adding two copies per cycle instead of doubling.

questions.stem: In gel electrophoresis, why do DNA fragments move through the gel towards the positive electrode?
options: The smallest fragments carry the largest charge
The gel pushes the fragments away from the wells
Their phosphate groups give them a negative charge
Their bases give them an overall positive charge
questions.explanation: Each nucleotide carries a negatively charged phosphate group, so DNA is attracted to the positive electrode. Charge per unit length is about the same for all fragments, so it is size, not charge, that sets how far a fragment travels: smaller fragments move further through the gel.

questions.stem: A child's DNA profile shows bands at 300 and 450 base pairs for one STR locus. The mother has bands at 300 and 520. Which possible father's bands are consistent with this child?
questions.explanation: A child inherits one STR allele from each parent. The 300 band can come from the mother, so the 450 band must come from the father, and only the man with a 450 band could be the father. Having bands identical to the mother's does not supply the 450 allele.

questions.stem: On a gel, a DNA ladder has bands at 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 base pairs. A sample band sits about halfway between the 200 and 300 bands. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The fragment moved faster than the 200 base pair band
The fragment is about 250 base pairs long
The fragment carries a stronger charge than the 200 band
The fragment is about 50 base pairs long
questions.explanation: Fragments are sized by comparison with a ladder run in the same gel, so a band between the 200 and 300 markers is about 250 base pairs. A 250 base pair fragment is larger than the 200 marker, so it moved more slowly, not faster. Strictly, distance is not linear with size, so this is an estimate.

questions.stem: In producing human insulin in bacteria, why are the plasmids designed to carry an antibiotic resistance gene?
options: So the plasmid can be cut open by the same restriction enzyme
So only bacteria that have taken up a plasmid survive on the antibiotic
So the insulin made by the bacteria is protected from bacterial enzymes
So the bacteria can splice introns out of the human insulin gene
questions.explanation: Transformation is inefficient, so bacteria are grown on a medium containing the antibiotic and only transformed cells survive. Bacteria cannot splice introns at all, which is why the inserted insulin sequence must have none.

questions.stem: Why is the human insulin gene inserted into plasmids as a sequence without introns, such as DNA made from mature mRNA?
options: Introns would stop restriction enzymes from cutting the plasmid
Bacteria have no splicing machinery to remove introns from pre-mRNA
Bacterial ribosomes read the genetic code differently from human ribosomes
Plasmids are too small to hold any gene that contains an intron
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes do not process RNA, so introns in a human gene would be translated and the protein would be wrong. The genetic code is universal, so bacterial ribosomes read human codons correctly; this is what makes the method work at all.

questions.stem: In the method used to make human insulin, bacteria produce the A and B chains in separate cultures. What happens next?
options: The chains are injected into patients as separate drugs
The chains are spliced together by RNA polymerase
The chains are purified and joined by disulfide bonds
The chains are inserted together into a single plasmid
questions.explanation: Each chain is made by a different population of transformed bacteria, extracted and purified, then the A and B chains are combined so disulfide bonds form between them, giving functional insulin. Neither chain works as a separate drug.

questions.stem: What makes an organism transgenic rather than only genetically modified?
options: It was produced by selective breeding over generations
It has had its whole genome copied by PCR
It carries a gene from a different species
It has had one of its own genes switched off
questions.explanation: All transgenic organisms are genetically modified, but transgenic specifically means a gene from another species has been inserted. An organism with one of its own genes knocked out, for example by CRISPR, is genetically modified but not transgenic.

questions.stem: Bt cotton, grown widely in Australia, carries a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. What benefit does this gene provide?
options: It increases the vitamin A content of the cotton seed
It produces a protein that is toxic to certain insect pests
It allows the plant to fix nitrogen gas from the air
It makes the plant resistant to a common viral disease
questions.explanation: The Bt gene codes for a Cry protein that kills caterpillar pests such as cotton bollworm when they eat the plant, so less insecticide is needed. Raising vitamin A content is the aim of Golden Rice, a different transgenic crop.
